title: String Indexing & Slicing
objective: Read individual characters and substrings out of a string using indexing and slicing.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Full Course for free
sourceAlignment.creator: Bro Code
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only; this topic isn't covered in Python Crash Course but is taught in the companion video. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A string is a sequence of characters, and Python lets you reach into that sequence the same way you would a list. word[0] gives you the first character, word[-1] gives you the last, and asking for an index that doesn't exist raises an IndexError, exactly like it does for lists.

A slice pulls out a whole substring instead of one character: word[1:4] returns a new string containing the characters at index 1 up to, but not including, index 4. Leaving off either number means 'to the start' or 'to the end', so word[:3] takes the first three characters and word[3:] takes everything after that.

Strings are immutable, so indexing and slicing only ever read characters — they never let you assign to word[0] the way you might with a list. To change part of a string, build a brand-new one instead, often by slicing and concatenating.
explanation.rule: word[i] reads one character by position; word[a:b] reads a substring from a up to (not including) b — neither one changes the original string.

examples.title: Reading Characters by Index
examples.note: word[0] is the first character; word[-1] is the last, no matter how long the string is.

examples.title: Slicing a Substring
examples.note: word[:4] takes the first four characters; word[4:] takes everything from index 4 onward.

feedback.incorrect: Count from index 1 up to, but not including, index 3: that's the characters at positions 1 and 2.

assignment.title: Shorten the Word
assignment.brief: Write shorten(word) that returns the first 3 characters of word if it's longer than 3 characters, otherwise returns word unchanged.
requirements: If len(word) is greater than 3, return word[:3].
assignment.starterCode:
def shorten(word):
    # Return the first 3 characters if word is longer than 3, else return word as-is.
    pass

print(shorten("hammer"))
print(shorten("ax"))

assignment.outputCheckLabel: shorten('hammer') and shorten('ax') print ham then ax

hints: word[:3] takes the first three characters of word.
len(word) tells you how long word is before you decide whether to shorten it.
If word has 3 or fewer characters, return it unchanged — don't slice it.
shorten('ax') should return 'ax' exactly, since it's not longer than 3 characters.
